title: Why Dolphin Pods Swell Every Late Summer
text:
When you browse Sarasota Bay’s dolphin sightings month by month, a striking seasonal rhythm emerges: groups are smallest in late winter and steadily grow all summer long. Across all 6,391 surveys conducted by the Sarasota Dolphin Research Program between 1971 and 2009, the average pod holds 3.84 dolphins in February, climbs through late spring and summer, and peaks at 6.02 dolphins in September—a 57% increase in group size. By September and October, more than 28% of all sightings involve large social groups of seven or more dolphins, nearly double February’s rate (15.6%).









At first glance, you might guess that outsiders swim into Sarasota Bay from the open Gulf each summer. Yet five decades of photo-identification and demographic tracking by Wells et al. (2025) rule that out: Sarasota Bay hosts a tightly knit resident community in which outside immigration is near zero (an annual rate of just 0.003 to 0.013). Instead, the late-summer surge comes from inside the community itself. Analyzing 482 resident dolphins, Wells and colleagues show that reproduction is sharply seasonal, with 81% of all births occurring between May and July.
Those newborn calves reshape how dolphins group together across the bay. Resident females—who can live up to 67 years, begin reproducing around age 9.6, and nurse each calf over an average 3.5-year calving interval—gather in warm, shallow seagrass meadows during summer and early autumn to form multi-mother nursery pods. Larger pods provide extra eyes against bull sharks, abundant summer prey, and social learning for calves during their most vulnerable first months of life, before groups disperse back into smaller foraging pairs and trios over the cooler winter months.

title: Bottlenose Dolphins of Sarasota Bay
text:
Since 1970, the Sarasota Dolphin Research Program (SDRP) has conducted the world’s longest-running study of a wild dolphin community. Drawing on 6,391 boat-based surveys (recording 30,980 individual dolphin observations from 1971 to 2009) alongside life-history findings from Wells et al. (2025), this site examines how Sarasota Bay’s resident bottlenose dolphins (Tursiops truncatus) shift their group sizes and locations across the months of the year.










Explore the Project

Monthly Sightings Explorer (Exploration): Filter the most recent five years of survey data (2005–2009) by month and year on an interactive map and monthly chart.
Summer Nurseries & Life History (Story): Why dolphin pods swell by nearly 60% from February to September—connecting our sighting records to 50+ years of calving and survival research.
